title: Milky Way
conditions: A clear dark sky, with the bright galactic region above the local horizon and no strong moonlight washing it out. Visibility depends on date, latitude and hemisphere.
intent: A recognisable Milky Way over a simple foreground, with stars close to points.

setup.focusTarget: Magnify a bright star in live view and turn the focus ring until its core is smallest. Check centre and corner stars in an enlarged recorded frame.
setup.stabilization: Use stabilisation handheld; on a locked tripod follow the lens/camera tripod guidance.
setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.
setup.exposureNote: Start at 10 s. Use the star estimator with actual focal length and pixel pitch. Shorten if stars stretch; raise ISO before extending a motion-limited shutter.

phone.mode: Astrophotography/night mode if available
phone.aperture: Fixed on most phones; not user adjustable.
phone.shutter: Automatic stack; 5–10 s only in a supported manual app
phone.focus: Lock distant focus and inspect an enlarged frame.
phone.guidance: Clamp the main camera and let a supported astro mode finish its sequence. Include a clean distant foreground edge.
phone.limitation: Night-mode duration often describes a stack, not one exposure. Manual ISO, focus and RAW depend on the phone and app.

why: Earth rotation limits the shutter even when the tripod is perfectly still.
A wide aperture gathers faint sky light while a wide field includes the galactic band.
A distant foreground may work at star focus; a nearby object can require a separately focused frame.
Fixed white balance keeps a sequence consistent; RAW retains colour-adjustment freedom.
steps: Check clouds, Moon position, darkness and galactic visibility for the exact location and date.
Choose a safe foreground in daylight and keep lamps out of the composition.
Secure the tripod, select RAW and focus manually on a magnified star.
Take the 10 s test and enlarge stars at the centre and corners.
Shorten shutter for directional trails; refocus round swollen stars; stop down slightly for wing-shaped corner aberrations.
If a near foreground is unsharp, make a separately focused frame and disclose any later blend.

problems.fix: Shorten shutter and raise ISO to restore brightness.
Refocus under magnification and inspect the front element.
Try f/3.2–4 and raise ISO while preserving shutter time.
Change location, direction or timing; avoid exposing the sky into clipping.

alternatives.effect: Similar brightness with less star movement, but possibly softer corners.
alternatives.requirements: An f/1.8 lens and careful corner inspection.

alternatives.name: Tracked sky
alternatives.effect: More sky signal while following star motion.
alternatives.requirements: Accurately aligned tracker; stationary foreground needs a separate capture and disclosed blend.

tip: Check corners as well as the centre: one sharp central star does not prove the whole wide-open frame is clean.
startingPoint: Test star shape in the recorded image before judging brightness. The listed exposure assumes a dark sky.

title: Pinpoint stars and constellations
conditions: A clear night with a recognisable constellation framed more tightly than a whole-sky nightscape.
intent: Small star points, visible star colour and a readable constellation pattern.

setup.focusTarget: Magnify a moderately bright star and minimise its diameter. Verify several recorded stars, not only the live view.
setup.stabilization: Use stabilisation handheld; on a locked tripod follow the lens/camera tripod guidance.
setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.
setup.exposureNote: At 50 mm start at 4 s and test. Pixel pitch, actual focal length, aperture and declination affect the limit; a wide-angle shutter cannot simply be reused.

phone.mode: Night mode or supported manual mode
phone.aperture: Fixed on most phones; not user adjustable.
phone.focus: Lock focus on a distant light or star.
phone.guidance: Use the main camera and a small landmark to establish direction. Reduce exposure if bright stars lose their colour.

why: A tighter field magnifies star motion, so the exposure is shorter than a wide nightscape.
A wide aperture helps keep the shutter short without excessive ISO.
Preserving bright-star highlights retains more colour than exposing every star to white.
steps: Use a local sky map to locate the pattern above obstructions.
Frame with enough margin to keep its geometry readable.
Manually focus on a magnified star and make a 4 s frame.
Inspect bright and faint stars at enlarged view.
Halve the shutter and double ISO for trails; lower exposure if bright stars clip.

title: Star trails
conditions: A clear night with a fixed foreground and at least half an hour available for consecutive exposures.
intent: Continuous star arcs around a celestial pole or broad sweeps away from it.

setup.focusTarget: Focus on a magnified star, inspect a test frame and leave manual focus unchanged for the sequence.
setup.stabilization: Use stabilisation handheld; on a locked tripod follow the lens/camera tripod guidance.
setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.
setup.exposureNote: Each 20 s frame belongs to a 30–90 minute sequence. Adjust ISO for sky brightness, minimise gaps and disable long-exposure dark-frame subtraction during the sequence.

phone.mode: Dedicated trail or interval app if available
phone.aperture: Fixed on most phones; not user adjustable.
phone.shutter: Repeated exposures controlled by the app
phone.focus: Lock focus and exposure before starting.
phone.guidance: Clamp the phone and use a true star-trail mode or save individual frames for later blending.
phone.limitation: Normal night mode usually aligns stars and suppresses trails; it is not equivalent to a trail mode.

why: Total sequence duration sets trail length; each frame’s exposure controls sky brightness.
Fixed focus, framing and white balance prevent discontinuities.
Long inter-frame gaps create dotted trails, especially with automatic dark frames.
The celestial-pole direction differs by hemisphere; pointing away creates sweeping arcs.
steps: Choose a pole-centred or sweeping-arc composition for the local sky.
Set a fixed foreground and check the weather for a sustained clear interval.
Focus manually and test one 20 s frame for sky clipping.
Set the shortest practical interval gap with sufficient battery and storage.
Capture at least 30 minutes without moving the rig.
Lighten-stack the series and inspect gaps, aircraft and passing lights.

essential: Interval timer or repeated timed capture

problems.fix: Shorten overhead and disable in-camera long-exposure dark frames.
Use solid ground and avoid touching the rig.
Lower ISO or shorten each frame while maintaining total sequence duration.
Protect against condensation and refocus between complete sequences.

alternatives.requirements: Dark sky and a lens with acceptable wide-open corners.

title: Full Moon detail
conditions: A clear uneclipsed full Moon reasonably high above the horizon and away from severe heat shimmer.
intent: A crisp lunar disc with dark maria and bright terrain below clipping.

setup.focusTarget: Focus with a small AF point on the lunar rim, then magnify and refine manually if needed.
setup.stabilization: Use stabilisation handheld; on a locked tripod follow the lens/camera tripod guidance.
setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.
setup.exposureNote: The Moon is sunlit. Begin at low ISO and a fast shutter; haze may require more ISO or 1/125 s. Inspect the bright surface, not the black sky.

phone.mode: Normal photo or supported manual telephoto mode
phone.aperture: Fixed on most phones; not user adjustable.
phone.focus: Tap and lock on the Moon.
phone.focal: Optical telephoto camera if fitted; avoid heavy digital zoom.
phone.guidance: Use a genuine optical telephoto camera and reduce exposure until the disc shows detail.
phone.limitation: The Moon stays small without optical reach; computational lunar enhancement is not captured optical detail.

why: The bright sunlit surface needs much less exposure than its black surroundings imply.
A fast shutter limits vibration and lunar drift at high magnification.
A higher Moon usually suffers less atmospheric disturbance than one near the horizon.
steps: Choose clear air and avoid looking over a hot roof.
Secure the long lens and leave margin around the lunar disc.
Focus on the rim and use a timer or remote.
Take a short series at 1/250 s.
Inspect terrain and edges enlarged; shorten exposure for clipping and compare frames for atmospheric steadiness.

essential: Long lens or suitable telescope adapter

problems.fix: Reduce ISO or shorten shutter in manual mode.
Wait for steadier air and take several frames.
Use delayed/remote release and a suitable shutter mode.
Use a longer lens or make an environmental composition.

alternatives.effect: Reduces vibration risk in a smaller lunar image.
alternatives.requirements: Effective stabilisation and steady technique.

alternatives.name: Short detail sequence

alternatives.requirements: Burst/stacking workflow with unclipped frames.

setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.

phone.shutter: Auto; shorten if the crescent clips
phone.focus: Lock on the bright crescent edge.

phone.limitation: Most phones show the phase more readily than fine crater relief.

why: Low-angle sunlight makes crater relief more visible than full-Moon lighting.
A moderate aperture avoids unnecessary diffraction.
Exposing for sunlit terrain deliberately leaves the unlit hemisphere dark.
steps: Check the phase and local altitude.
Frame the terminator with margin for lunar movement.
Focus on a magnified lit crater rim.
Take several 1/125 s test frames.
Inspect shadow boundaries for focus, vibration and clipping before changing ISO.

Use the earthshine sheet if the faint side is the goal.
Take a sequence and choose the sharpest frame.
Use delayed release and stiffen support.

title: Moon in a landscape
conditions: A rising or setting Moon during twilight, with enough remaining light to record the landscape.
intent: A naturally scaled Moon aligned with a distant ridge, tree or building.

setup.focusTarget: Focus on a genuinely distant landmark and check the Moon too. If both cannot be sharp, stop down or choose a more distant foreground.
setup.stabilization: Use stabilisation handheld; on a locked tripod follow the lens/camera tripod guidance.
setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.
setup.exposureNote: Start by retaining detail in the sunlit lunar disc. Twilight narrows the brightness gap but may still leave the land dark. If needed, make a separate longer exposure for the foreground at the same framing and focal length, and disclose the blend. Increase lunar exposure only if actual haze dims the disc; inspect its highlights.

phone.mode: Normal photo with exposure lock
phone.aperture: Fixed on most phones; not user adjustable.
phone.shutter: Auto; avoid long lunar night stacks
phone.focus: Focus on the distant skyline.
phone.guidance: Use optical telephoto while the sky still has colour and lower exposure enough to retain lunar shape.

Moving farther from the foreground allows a longer lens to make the Moon larger relative to it.
A short shutter preserves the lunar edge at telephoto magnification.

Choose a distant foreground and safe position before twilight.
Focus and verify both landmark and Moon.
Test exposure for the lunar disc.

title: Aurora curtains
conditions: Visible auroral curtains under clear dark skies, changing shape within seconds.
intent: Distinct rays and folds above a grounded foreground rather than a smooth green wash.

setup.stabilization: Use stabilisation handheld; on a locked tripod follow the lens/camera tripod guidance.
setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.

A wide view leaves room for a changing overhead display.
Higher ISO preserves shape when there is no time for a longer exposure.

Set a wide composition with a simple horizon.
Focus manually on a star and test at 2 s.
Enlarge the rays and check bright colour channels.
Shorten for fast curtains and extend only for a faint slow arc.

title: Meteor shower
conditions: A meteor-shower period with clear dark skies and the radiant above the local horizon.
intent: A meteor streak across recognisable stars, found in a long repeating capture sequence.

steps: Check shower timing, radiant altitude, Moon and weather for the exact location.
Choose a wide sky patch away from local lights.
Focus on a star and test sharpness at 8 s.
Run a sustained sequence with minimum practical gap.
Inspect occasional frames for dew and sky brightness without moving the rig.
Review individual files later and compare adjacent frames to identify aircraft.

title: Lunar eclipse totality
conditions: The Moon is within Earth’s umbra, with brightness ranging from orange-red to very dark brown.

setup.stabilization: Use stabilisation handheld; on a locked tripod follow the lens/camera tripod guidance.
setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.

phone.aperture: Fixed on most phones; not user adjustable.
phone.shutter: Shortest useful capture for the dark disc

Set up and focus during the bright partial phase.
At totality, test the listed exposure and bracket.
Enlarge rim and crater detail to separate motion from noise.
Use higher ISO for a shorter time or a tracker for substantially longer exposures.
Return to short exposures as direct sunlight reappears.

why: Earthshine is much fainter than the sunlit crescent, so the exposure goal differs from crater-detail photography.
Twilight balances sky brightness against a Moon that may be low on the horizon.
Moderate telephoto reach limits the effect of lunar drift compared with very long focal lengths.
steps: Check thin-crescent visibility, rise/set time and the real local horizon.
Set up before twilight fades and focus on the bright edge.
Test a 1/4 s frame for the faint hemisphere.
Inspect its detail and noise separately from the possibly clipped crescent.
Capture a short companion exposure if blending, retaining the same scale and framing.

problems.fix: Increase exposure for earthshine or bracket the two brightness levels.
Clean/shade the lens and try clearer air; more exposure can worsen it.
Use timer/remote and firmer support.
Shorten exposure and raise ISO.

alternatives.requirements: Same framing; disclose any later exposure blend.

title: Sunrise reflected in water
conditions: A calm shoreline just before or after sunrise, with coloured sky reflected in gentle ripples.
intent: A balanced sky-and-water composition with visible reflection texture.

why: Moderate aperture keeps shoreline and reflection readable.
A shortish shutter preserves ripples instead of turning the reflection into an anonymous wash.
Daylight white balance preserves the warm colour rather than neutralising it.
steps: Arrive before local sunrise and choose a sheltered stretch of water.
Balance sky and reflection; a centred horizon can work when the symmetry is deliberate.
Focus on a distant edge and expose a 1/30 s test.
Check bright clouds and their reflection for clipped colour.
Shorten shutter as the Sun rises, or extend it deliberately if you want smoother water.

problems.fix: Reduce/remove polarisation and change camera height.
Shorten shutter or bracket for a darker sky frame.

Refocus on the distant shore and check depth of field.

why: The dark subject is intentional; its outline must carry the information.

A tighter lens simplifies the sky and removes clutter around the shape.
steps: Choose an immediately recognisable outline and a clear sky behind it.
Move sideways or lower the camera to separate overlapping limbs and branches.
Focus on the edge and take the starting exposure.
Inspect the silhouette boundary for mergers and the sky for clipped colour.
Adjust shutter for sky brightness; keep the subject dark unless you intentionally change the effect.

setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.

The fast shutter protects the thin subject from wind movement.

steps: Find low sun behind the plant and a naturally darker background.
Shift the camera so direct glare is blocked by the subject or excluded from the frame.
Focus on one important seed head and take a test at 1/500 s.

Raise shutter in wind or lower ISO if illuminated edges clip.

title: Blue-hour coastline

setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.

why: The tripod allows low ISO while twilight becomes dim.
A several-second exposure softens small waves but keeps fixed rocks crisp.
A consistent cool white balance preserves the blue-hour mood.
steps: Check tides and a safe dry route before darkness.
Frame a strong rock or coastline line against the open water.
Focus before the scene becomes too dim for reliable AF.
Make a 4 s frame with a timer.
Check horizon, rock sharpness and bright lights; extend exposure only as the ambient light falls.

title: Sunburst through a gap
conditions: A bright small portion of the Sun peeking around a tree, rock or building edge.
intent: Defined diffraction rays around a partly hidden light source, with usable foreground detail.

setup.focusTarget: Focus on the foreground object forming the gap, then inspect the distant detail. Do not focus by looking directly at the Sun.
setup.stabilization: Use stabilisation handheld; on a locked tripod follow the lens/camera tripod guidance.
setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.
setup.exposureNote: f/16 promotes rays but can soften fine detail by diffraction. Meter a test for the surrounding sky, bracket if needed, and keep direct solar exposure brief.

phone.mode: Normal photo
phone.aperture: Fixed on most phones; not user adjustable.
phone.focus: Tap the edge partly covering the Sun.
phone.guidance: Hide most of the Sun behind an edge and try a tiny sideways movement to reveal a small point.
phone.limitation: Most phones have a fixed wide aperture and will not produce the same diaphragm sunburst; optical flare is not the same effect.

why: A small aperture forms diffraction spikes whose shape depends on the lens diaphragm.
Partly hiding the Sun limits the bright area and makes the rays more defined.
f/16 is an effect choice, with a trade-off in fine-detail sharpness.
steps: Choose a solid edge that can hide almost all of the Sun.
Compose using the rear screen with only a brief small glimpse of direct sunlight.
Set f/16 and focus on the masking edge.
Move slightly until rays emerge, then take the test promptly.
Check flare, clipping and overall sharpness; compare f/11 if diffraction is excessive.

problems.cause: Aperture wide or light source too large
problems.fix: Try f/11–16 and hide more of the source behind the edge.
Change angle slightly and clean the front element.

problems.cause: Diffraction from a very small aperture
problems.fix: Compare f/11 and avoid stopping beyond what the effect needs.
Bracket for a blend or change composition to use a silhouette.

alternatives.requirements: Lens-specific; compare both apertures.

startingPoint: Test briefly, inspect flare and compare f/11 with f/16 instead of assuming the smallest aperture is best.
safety: Never look directly at the Sun or through an optical viewfinder at it. Keep framing brief using a screen and avoid prolonged direct solar aiming; use proper solar filtration for dedicated solar imaging.

title: Sunrise through sea mist
conditions: Low mist over calm water as warm sunrise light starts to filter through it.
intent: Soft luminous layers and a readable focal shape without forcing the mist into heavy contrast.

phone.mode: Normal photo
phone.aperture: Fixed on most phones; not user adjustable.
phone.focus: Tap a distinct object in front of the mist.

The low-contrast mist should remain luminous rather than being forced to middle grey.
Focusing on a solid object is more reliable than focusing on the mist itself.
steps: Find a viewpoint where mist separates two or more depth layers.
Choose a simple boat, post or rock as the anchor.
Focus on that anchor and test the starting exposure.
Inspect bright mist for texture and the anchor for sharpness.
Adjust shutter or ISO as the Sun strengthens; preserve the gentle contrast.

problems.fix: Increase exposure cautiously in manual mode while checking highlights.

problems.fix: Move the AF point to a solid edge or focus manually.
Use a longer lens or crop a simpler layered section.

Choose a simple lower-edge silhouette to give scale.
Focus at distance and test 1/125 s.
Check coloured highlights, then shorten exposure if their texture disappears.
Continue into the afterglow and adjust shutter or ISO as light fades.

Use fixed Daylight and judge exposure with a test.

A moderate small aperture balances depth with diffraction.

Level and secure the camera; remove unimportant very close intrusions.
Focus beyond the nearest object and take the starting frame.

Focus on the anchor edge and test the exposure.

title: Lightning from enclosed shelter

alternatives.name: Gentle smooth current
alternatives.effect: Longer lines show a slower stream’s direction.
alternatives.requirements: Two extra stops of ND versus 1/8 s in unchanged light.

tip: Trigger as a small patch of foam enters the strongest curve; it can turn invisible motion into a readable leading line.
startingPoint: Use the first frame to judge streak length, then change shutter and compensate exposure deliberately.
safety: Work from secure ground and keep out of fast or unexpectedly deep water.

title: Frozen fountain droplets
conditions: A sunlit fountain with bright droplets against a darker background.
intent: Distinct beads and arcs of water instead of blurred spray.

setup.focusTarget: Use a small continuous AF area on a consistent part of the arc, or pre-focus manually where droplets repeatedly pass.
setup.stabilization: Use stabilisation handheld; on a locked tripod follow the lens/camera tripod guidance.
setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.
setup.exposureNote: Keep at least about 1/2000 s for small fast droplets. Raise ISO before slowing shutter; brighter light or side/backlighting makes individual drops easier to see.

phone.mode: Normal photo burst in bright light; manual if available
phone.aperture: Fixed on most phones; not user adjustable.
phone.focus: Tap the repeated water arc or nearby nozzle at the same distance.
phone.focal: Optical telephoto if fitted; main lens otherwise.
phone.guidance: Choose bright daylight and a dark background, then shoot a short burst.
phone.limitation: The phone may choose a slower shutter automatically; burst alone does not freeze droplets.

why: Very short exposure separates individual droplets.
A dark background and side/backlight reveal transparent water.
Moderate aperture gives some depth across the arc while keeping ISO manageable.
steps: Find a safe dry viewpoint with sunlight catching the water from the side or back.
Place the brightest droplets against a dark background.
Focus on a repeatable part of the water arc.
Shoot a short burst at 1/2000 s.
Inspect droplet edges: raise shutter for streaks, refine focus if the whole plane is soft.

problems.fix: Use 1/4000 s and raise ISO.
Prefocus on the arc plane or use a smaller AF area.
Change position for dark background and side/backlight.
Retain surrounding droplet edges; lower exposure if too much of each drop is lost.

alternatives.name: Long luminous water arcs
alternatives.effect: Droplets merge into continuous curved lines.
alternatives.requirements: Tripod and sufficient ND in bright daylight.

alternatives.name: More arc depth
alternatives.effect: More droplets across the depth of the jet appear sharp.
alternatives.requirements: More ISO or stronger light.

tip: Watch the backdrop before the water. A small sideways move can make transparent droplets suddenly visible.
startingPoint: Take a burst and inspect individual droplets at full size; a bright preview can hide motion streaks.

title: Breaking waves and flying spray
conditions: Daylight waves breaking offshore or against rocks, photographed from a safe position beyond the largest wave reach.
intent: A sharply defined crest with suspended spray and a sense of force.

setup.focusTarget: Track the crest with a medium AF area, or pre-focus on the predictable break zone if autofocus jumps to nearer spray.
setup.stabilization: Use stabilisation handheld; on a locked tripod follow the lens/camera tripod guidance.
setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.
setup.exposureNote: Start at 1/2000 s for spray. Increase ISO in cloud rather than letting shutter fall; shorten further if individual droplets still streak at tight framing.

phone.mode: Normal photo burst; optical telephoto if available
phone.aperture: Fixed on most phones; not user adjustable.
phone.shutter: Auto; fast shutter needs bright light
phone.focus: Tap the break zone and use burst.
phone.guidance: Stay well back and use optical reach; time the burst just before the crest collapses.
phone.limitation: A phone cannot compensate for an unsafe viewpoint, and digital zoom reduces spray detail.

why: A fast shutter preserves the explosion of spray.
A telephoto lens gives framing flexibility from safer distances.
A little depth of field helps when the crest and spray occupy different distances.
steps: Observe several wave sets from well beyond their reach before setting up.
Choose a break zone with a clean dark or contrasting background.
Track the crest or pre-focus on where it repeatedly breaks.
Start a short burst just before the wave collapses.
Check spray sharpness and white-water clipping, then adjust shutter or ISO.

problems.symptom: Spray is blurred but rocks sharp
problems.fix: Use a faster shutter.

problems.symptom: Nearest spray sharp, main crest soft
problems.fix: Use a smaller/selected AF area or pre-focus at the break zone.
Reduce ISO or shorten shutter.
Watch the swell shape and begin slightly before the peak.

alternatives.name: Wave motion lines
alternatives.effect: A dynamic sweep rather than frozen spray.
alternatives.requirements: Tripod, safe location and metered ND as needed.

alternatives.name: Tighter spray detail
alternatives.effect: Smaller droplets and fast fragments remain distinct.
alternatives.requirements: Telephoto lens; narrower depth and more ISO noise.

tip: The largest wave in a set may arrive after several ordinary ones. Choose your position for the largest plausible wave, not the last one you watched.
startingPoint: Test sharpness and white-water detail from your safe position; keep checking the changing sea.
safety: Keep well beyond the largest expected wave reach and away from unstable cliff edges. Do not turn your back on the sea while moving.

title: Rain streaks in backlight
conditions: Rain visible in side or backlight against a dark background, photographed from secure shelter.
intent: Readable diagonal rain lines while the main static subject remains sharp.

setup.focusTarget: Focus on the fixed subject or background plane where the rain is most visible; do not let AF jump between near droplets.
setup.whiteBalance: Daylight for daylight rain; fixed to suit artificial light
setup.stabilization: Use stabilisation handheld; on a locked tripod follow the lens/camera tripod guidance.
setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.
setup.exposureNote: Start at 1/60 s for visible streaks. Use 1/30 s for longer lines or 1/250 s for shorter ones; compensate ISO/aperture rather than treating rain speed as an exposure meter.

phone.mode: Normal photo or manual shutter app
phone.aperture: Fixed on most phones; not user adjustable.
phone.focus: Tap the fixed subject and lock focus.
phone.guidance: Work under shelter with a dark background and light shining through the rain.
phone.limitation: Automatic phones may choose a faster shutter and make rain less visible; night stacks can remove or distort streaks.

why: Side/backlight makes otherwise transparent drops visible.
A medium-slow shutter stretches falling drops into readable lines.
A darker background gives those lines contrast without needing extreme processing.
steps: Choose shelter that keeps both you and the equipment out of hazardous weather.
Find rain crossing a dark backdrop with side or rear illumination.
Focus on a fixed object and steady the camera.
Take a 1/60 s test and inspect streak length.
Change shutter for the desired line length, then compensate exposure and check the static subject.

problems.fix: Move the view toward side-lit rain against a darker background.
Use support; rain alone should streak.

problems.cause: Drops too close to the lens or water on glass
problems.fix: Reframe away from nearby drops and clean the lens safely.

problems.symptom: Rain lines too long and dense
problems.cause: Shutter too slow for rainfall rate
problems.fix: Shorten toward 1/125–1/250 s.

alternatives.name: Short textured rain
alternatives.effect: Shorter dashes retain more of the subject’s visibility.
alternatives.requirements: More ISO or brighter backlight.

alternatives.name: Long dramatic lines
alternatives.effect: Longer rain streaks across a static subject.
alternatives.requirements: Firm support and no subject movement that must remain sharp.

tip: One illuminated strip of rain against a dark doorway or tree can read more clearly than an entire bright rainy landscape.
startingPoint: Test rain visibility and the static subject separately; choose streak length first, then correct exposure.
safety: If thunder is heard, move inside substantial enclosed shelter; a canopy or open porch is not lightning protection.

title: Long-exposure seascape
conditions: A stable shoreline scene with fixed rocks or a pier and moving water; dim twilight or suitable ND filtration.
intent: Smooth sea around crisp fixed forms, with a calm and simplified composition.

setup.focus: AF-S then MF · fixed shoreline edge
setup.focusTarget: Focus on a fixed rock or pier before adding a dense ND filter; switch to manual focus to prevent hunting through the filter.
setup.stabilization: Use stabilisation handheld; on a locked tripod follow the lens/camera tripod guidance.
setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.
setup.exposureNote: Thirty seconds is an effect target, not a universal exposure. Meter without ND, then calculate required filter stops; during twilight retest because light changes while you work.

phone.mode: Supported long-exposure effect/app
phone.aperture: Fixed on most phones; not user adjustable.
phone.shutter: Stacked effect, or genuine manual exposure if supported
phone.focus: Lock focus on a fixed shoreline object.
phone.guidance: Mount the phone and use a long-exposure mode designed to blur water while keeping fixed features.
phone.limitation: Most phones cannot make a genuine 30 s exposure in daylight; a stacking effect may show artifacts.

why: Long exposure averages many small waves into broad smooth tones.
Fixed objects provide visual structure when moving water loses detail.
Dense ND controls exposure while preserving a moderate aperture and low ISO.
steps: Check tide and swell, then place the tripod on stable ground beyond the wash.
Build the composition around one or two fixed forms.
Focus and meter without a dense ND filter.
Fit the filter, calculate the new time and use a timer or remote for the 30 s test.
Check rock sharpness, horizon level, highlight clipping and any colour cast.
Recalculate after light changes; adjust time for texture rather than simply making every frame longer.

essential: Manual exposure with a timer/remote for the chosen duration
optional: Viewfinder cover if the camera admits stray light during long exposures

problems.fix: Use stable ground and prevent wave contact.
Try 2–5 s or add a stronger fixed subject.

problems.cause: Insufficient ND for the desired time
problems.fix: Calculate a stronger ND or shoot in dimmer light.
Try another filter/angle, shade stray light and correct a moderate cast from RAW.

alternatives.name: Directional surf
alternatives.effect: Retains long wave lines instead of a completely smooth surface.
alternatives.requirements: About four fewer ND stops than a 30 s frame in unchanged light; meter exactly.

alternatives.name: Minimal calm surface
alternatives.effect: Averages more waves and can simplify moving clouds.
alternatives.requirements: Remote Bulb/timed mode and roughly two extra ND stops versus 30 s.

tip: Take an unfiltered reference frame. It records real colour and lets you see exactly what the long exposure changed.
startingPoint: Meter first and calculate filtration; use a test exposure to verify both brightness and water texture.
safety: Check tide, swell and the return route. Keep the tripod and yourself beyond wave wash; do not leave equipment where retrieval would become hazardous.

title: Abstract moving reflections
conditions: Coloured buildings, foliage or lights reflected in gently moving water, with bright daylight or strong illumination.
intent: A frame of fluid colour shapes and repeating distorted lines, without literal scene context.

setup.focusTarget: Focus on a recognisable reflected edge, not on floating debris closer to the camera. Verify the intended reflection plane.
setup.whiteBalance: Daylight or fixed to suit reflected lights
setup.stabilization: Use stabilisation handheld; on a locked tripod follow the lens/camera tripod guidance.
setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.
setup.exposureNote: Start at 1/500 s to hold ripple shapes. Use a slower shutter deliberately for painterly blending; adjust ISO as illumination changes.

phone.mode: Normal photo burst
phone.aperture: Fixed on most phones; not user adjustable.
phone.focus: Tap a high-contrast reflected edge.
phone.focal: Optical telephoto if fitted, or main lens with a tight composition.
phone.guidance: Fill the frame with reflection alone and turn the phone until the line rhythm feels deliberate.
phone.limitation: Night modes can blend changing ripples into a different effect; use normal capture for defined shapes.

why: A fast shutter preserves the constantly changing abstract pattern.
A longer lens isolates colour and removes the literal object above the water.
Fixed white balance keeps a series of colour studies comparable.
steps: Look for strong colour reflected into water with small ripples.
Exclude the actual subject and shoreline if the abstraction is the goal.
Focus on the reflection and take a short burst.
Inspect whether the shapes are sharp enough and whether bright glints dominate.
Change viewpoint or timing for better rhythm before changing saturation.

optional: Support for a slower abstract variation

problems.symptom: Reflection turns into a uniform smear
problems.cause: Shutter too slow for the desired defined pattern
problems.fix: Use 1/500 s or faster.

problems.symptom: Floating debris sharp, colour shapes soft
problems.fix: Focus on a reflected edge.
Change viewpoint or reduce exposure.

problems.symptom: Image looks random rather than composed
problems.cause: No clear rhythm or colour anchor
problems.fix: Crop around a repeated line and one contrasting colour.

alternatives.name: Painterly blended colour
alternatives.effect: Ripples merge into broader brushlike forms.
alternatives.requirements: Support and metered ND if bright.

alternatives.name: Crisp tiny ripples
alternatives.effect: Sharper small facets and broken colour shapes.
alternatives.requirements: Bright reflections and careful focus.

tip: Rotate the final image only if the abstraction benefits; first keep a reference frame that shows what was reflected.
startingPoint: Take several test frames because the pattern changes continuously; choose both exposure and a coherent shape.

title: Moving boat on water
conditions: A boat moving across daylight water, photographed from stable shore or a securely supported platform.
intent: A sharp vessel with a readable wake and enough space in its direction of travel.

setup.focusTarget: Track a solid high-contrast part of the boat rather than splashing wake; use a medium AF area that stays on the vessel.
setup.stabilization: Use stabilisation handheld; on a locked tripod follow the lens/camera tripod guidance.
setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.
setup.exposureNote: Keep 1/1000 s for ordinary moving boats and raise ISO in shade. For fast craft or shooting from another moving boat, increase to 1/2000 s; stabilisation does not freeze the subject.

phone.mode: Normal photo burst with optical telephoto if available
phone.aperture: Fixed on most phones; not user adjustable.
phone.shutter: Auto; bright light helps freeze the boat
phone.focus: Track/tap the vessel rather than the wake.
phone.guidance: Leave space ahead of travel and shoot a short burst as the boat reaches a clean background.
phone.limitation: Digital zoom and automatic slow shutter limit detail; avoid leaning or unsafe positions for framing.

why: A fast shutter manages both vessel movement and possible platform movement.
Tracking the solid boat gives AF a more stable target than sparkling water.
Space ahead and a visible wake make direction immediately readable.
steps: Choose a safe stable viewpoint and watch the boat’s route.
Frame with room ahead and enough wake behind to show movement.
Acquire continuous focus on the cabin or hull before the desired moment.
Shoot a short burst at 1/1000 s.
Inspect the vessel edge for motion and the wake for clipping; raise shutter/ISO if needed.

optional: Safety equipment required for any boat you are aboard

problems.fix: Keep the AF area on a solid cabin/hull feature.

problems.cause: Shutter too slow for relative movement
problems.fix: Use 1/2000 s or faster and raise ISO.

problems.symptom: Boat seems about to leave the frame
problems.fix: Track earlier and frame with lead room.
Increase shutter, stabilise safely and level the horizon.

alternatives.name: Panned boat
alternatives.effect: Boat partly sharp with streaked water and background.
alternatives.requirements: Smooth tracking from a stable safe position; many attempts and ND in bright light.

alternatives.name: Fast powerboat spray
alternatives.effect: Sharper high-speed hull and flying wake droplets.
alternatives.requirements: Bright light or higher ISO as needed.

tip: Wait for a background gap before firing the burst; a sharp boat against a busy shoreline can still be hard to read.
startingPoint: Take a test pass and inspect the vessel itself, not only the wake, before committing to a slower shutter.
safety: Use a safe viewpoint. If aboard a vessel, follow crew instructions and applicable flotation requirements; do not compromise balance to frame the shot.
